name: Stoicism
summary: Stoicism is the Hellenistic school founded by Zeno of Citium around 300 BCE, holding that virtue, the perfection of reason, is the only good and is sufficient for happiness, while wealth, health and status are 'indifferents' to be used well. Its political implications come from the claims that all rational beings share one law of reason and are fellow citizens of a single world city, that humans are social animals with duties to serve the common good, and that the wise should take part in public life. It shaped the natural-law tradition and later cosmopolitan thought, but it never set out a policy program.
scope: Stoicism as a philosophy, with political implications drawn as its scholars (the Stanford and Internet Encyclopedias of Philosophy) and its Roman sources draw them: Marcus Aurelius's Meditations and Cicero's De Officiis, which follows the Stoic Panaetius. Modern Stoicism (the Modern Stoicism community) is used only to show where today's adherents agree or divide. Zeno's lost Republic and Cynic-leaning early Stoicism are not the basis. Most modern policy questions are inferences from principles and are marked low confidence; many are answered as split because the school is not a political theory.

sources.usedFor: Common reason implies common law and a world-state of fellow citizens; humans exist for one another; acceptance of change.

sources.title: Stoics Do Care about Social Justice: A Response to Irvine
sources.author: Eric O. Scott (Modern Stoicism)
sources.usedFor: Modern adherents' range of political views; Stoicism as not a political theory; debate over hate-speech laws and justice.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Health is a preferred indifferent and Stoicism does not say who should provide it; modern Stoics can be progressive or conservative, so this is inferred as split.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Stoicism prescribes no economic program; ancient Stoics treated wealth as a preferred indifferent and modern adherents span left and right on this, so it is inferred as split.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Stoicism prescribes no economic program; ancient Stoics treated wealth as a preferred indifferent and modern adherents span left and right on this, so it is inferred as split.

public-ownership.rationale: Cicero separates common goods used for the common interest from private goods but names no industries; the school has no view on which should be public.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Stoicism prescribes no economic program; ancient Stoics treated wealth as a preferred indifferent and modern adherents span left and right on this, so it is inferred as split.

unions-good.rationale: Nothing in Stoic ethics addresses organized labor, and modern adherents disagree on such questions, so this is inferred as split.

property-fundamental.rationale: In the Stoic-derived De Officiis property is conventional rather than natural, but once assigned each should keep his own and taking more violates human fellowship.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Stoicism prescribes no economic program; ancient Stoics treated wealth as a preferred indifferent and modern adherents span left and right on this, so it is inferred as split.

cut-welfare.rationale: Inferred from the teaching that rational beings exist for one another and from Cicero's call to share resources generously; welfare as such is not discussed.

worker-ownership.rationale: Stoicism prescribes no economic program; ancient Stoics treated wealth as a preferred indifferent and modern adherents span left and right on this, so it is inferred as split.

surveillance-ok.rationale: No Stoic principle settles this trade-off; inferred as split, since security and the freedom of the governed are both valued.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Stoics prize self-mastery over pleasures but distinguish personal virtue from law, and say nothing on prohibition; inferred as split.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: The teaching that insults harm only if we judge them harmful leads prominent modern Stoics such as Irvine to oppose hate-speech laws, though others in the community dissent.

strong-leader.rationale: Roman Stoics such as Cato resisted Caesar's bid for supremacy and Cicero condemns that ambition; Marcus's ideal ruler governs under the same law for all and respects the freedom of the governed.

state-harmful.rationale: Stoics, unlike Epicureans, urged engagement in public life and did not think harmony with the cosmos required distance from actual cities.

limit-guns.rationale: Not addressed by Stoic sources or principles in any direction; inferred as split.

empower-police-military.rationale: Not addressed; Stoic principles of justice and duty do not settle funding levels, so it is inferred as split.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Musonius held men and women to the same sexual standards, but Stoics did not frame this as law; legality is inferred as split.

decide-locally.rationale: Stoics combine duties to the world city with acknowledged duties to one's own city, and do not rank levels of government.

rehabilitation.rationale: Stoics see wrongdoing as error from ignorance and anger as a false judgment, so wrongdoers should be tolerated and taught rather than raged at.

traditional-family.rationale: Oikeiosis starts its circles of concern with the family, and later Stoics urged marriage and household duties, though Zeno's early Republic was more radical.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Ancient Stoics did not address it and modern adherents have no shared view; inferred as split.

abortion-legal.rationale: Not settled by the sources read; modern adherents have no shared position, so it is inferred as split.

more-religion-public.rationale: Stoics identified god with the rational cosmos rather than a cult or church, and modern Stoicism is largely secular; there is no call for more or less religion in public life.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Modern adherents such as Scott argue that the virtue of justice and the equality of all rational beings require working against racial injustice, though some in the community reject the framing.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Musonius held women capable of virtue and philosophy equally with men, but the Stoics made no claim about gender being constructed; inferred as split.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Roman Stoics kept duties to Rome alongside duties to the cosmopolis, while treating custom as secondary to universal reason; this balances to neutral.

gradual-change.rationale: Inferred from the Stoic acceptance of what happens and Cicero's institutional, duty-based politics rather than any revolutionary program.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Inferred from cosmopolitanism: all rational beings are fellow citizens of one world city, and helping people abroad is part of serving humanity.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Inferred from the idea of a common law and a world-state of reason, though the Stoics proposed no world government.

free-trade.rationale: Not addressed by Stoic sources; inferred as split.

nation-first.rationale: Justice extends to all human beings and not only to one's own community, though Roman Stoics gave their country a real but limited claim.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Cicero allows war only to secure peace without injury and binds it by rules; whether that covers protecting others is not settled, so it is inferred as split.

open-borders.rationale: Inferred from the claim that every rational being is a citizen of the world city, though no Stoic proposed abolishing borders.

limit-growth.rationale: Inferred from the view that wealth is merely a preferred indifferent and from Stoic praise of simple living; modern Stoic writers apply this to the environment.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Inferred from the duty to serve the common good of all humanity; modern adherents disagree on politics but many apply Stoic justice to climate.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: For Stoics the chief human problems lie in false judgments and vice, and only virtue secures happiness; external tools are indifferents.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Anachronistic and not implied by any Stoic principle; inferred as split.

revolution-justified.rationale: Stoics accepted fate yet some, like Cato, fought tyranny and others were persecuted for opposing emperors; there is no settled view on revolution.

experts-over-public.rationale: Only the sage has knowledge, so Stoics favored rule by the wise, though they never framed it as experts versus the public.

central-planning.rationale: Stoicism prescribes no economic program; ancient Stoics treated wealth as a preferred indifferent and modern adherents span left and right on this, so it is inferred as split.

socialized-markets.rationale: Stoicism prescribes no economic program; ancient Stoics treated wealth as a preferred indifferent and modern adherents span left and right on this, so it is inferred as split.

land-value-tax.rationale: No Stoic principle bears on tax design; inferred as split.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Stoicism prescribes no economic program; ancient Stoics treated wealth as a preferred indifferent and modern adherents span left and right on this, so it is inferred as split.

basic-income.rationale: Stoicism prescribes no economic program; ancient Stoics treated wealth as a preferred indifferent and modern adherents span left and right on this, so it is inferred as split.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Not addressed by Stoic sources; inferred as split.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Stoicism prescribes no economic program; ancient Stoics treated wealth as a preferred indifferent and modern adherents span left and right on this, so it is inferred as split.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Stoics accept property as conventional and value simplicity but propose no pattern of distribution; inferred as split.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Mainstream Roman Stoicism accepts property and conventional economic life as material for virtue rather than seeking to abolish it.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Anachronistic and not implied by Stoic principles; inferred as split.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Not addressed by Stoic sources; inferred as split.

one-party-rule.rationale: Inferred from Marcus's ideal of a polity under the same law for all with freedom for the governed, and from the Stoic distrust of partisanship.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Marcus Aurelius, himself an emperor, praises a kingly government that respects the freedom of the governed; Stoics judged rulers by justice, not form.

democracy-best.rationale: Marcus's ideal pairs equal law and free speech with kingship, and Stoics judged constitutions by justice rather than by form, so this is inferred as split.

direct-votes.rationale: Inferred from the Stoic view that knowledge belongs to the wise; the Stoics showed no preference for direct democracy.

workers-councils.rationale: Inferred: Stoic politics works through existing civic institutions and offices, with no class-based organs of power.

right-to-secede.rationale: Not addressed by Stoic sources; inferred as split.

natural-rulers.rationale: Stoics hold only the sage is truly fit to rule, yet every human shares reason and can in principle become wise; adherents read this both ways.

political-violence-never.rationale: Cicero allows just war, and Stoics like Cato took up arms against Caesar's tyranny, so violence is not ruled out in all cases.

war-builds-character.rationale: Cicero says war is waged only to live in peace without injury, so it is a means, not a school of national character.

separate-church-state.rationale: Stoics had no church; their god is the rational cosmos, so the question is anachronistic and inferred as split.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: For the Stoics true law is right reason pervading nature, knowable by any rational being, not a revealed text.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Inferred from the Stoic duty to serve the common good through public office and civic life.

military-superiority.rationale: Inferred from Cicero's view that war is justified only to secure peace and from cosmopolitan concern for all peoples.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Stoic cosmopolitanism grounds citizenship in shared reason, making every rational being a fellow citizen regardless of origin.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Stoics see events as unfolding through a rational, providential order (logos), not class conflict.

equal-outcomes.rationale: External goods are indifferent to happiness and Cicero tells each to keep what falls to him, so equalizing them is not a Stoic aim.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Not addressed by Stoic sources; inferred as split.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Not addressed by Stoic sources; modern adherents differ, so it is inferred as split.

civilizational-union.rationale: The Stoic community is all of rational humanity, not one religion or civilization.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Cicero, following Panaetius, says we are not born for ourselves alone, and only virtue, not personal advantage, is good.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Stoic ethics is built on duties (officia) to family, country and humanity; it has no doctrine of individual rights.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: The cosmos is divine and rational in Stoic physics, though Stoics also held reason sets humans above animals; inferred.

limit-population.rationale: Not addressed by Stoic sources; inferred as split.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Inferred: Stoics locate harm in judgments rather than in external conditions, and accept change as nature's way.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Inferred from the view that externals are indifferent and that virtue, not technical progress, is what matters.

human-enhancement.rationale: Anachronistic; Stoic principles could be read either way, so it is inferred as split.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Anachronistic and not settled by Stoic principles; inferred as split.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: Anachronistic and not settled by Stoic principles; inferred as split.

restore-past-order.rationale: Stoics teach acceptance that the universe is constant transformation, not nostalgia for a lost order.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Following Panaetius, Cicero holds that what is morally right outranks the merely expedient, so policies are judged first by justice.

direct-action.rationale: Stoics urged taking part in public life and holding office, which points to working through institutions; inferred from their ethic of civic service.

means-match-ends.rationale: For Stoics only virtuous action is good and outcomes are indifferent, so a good end cannot excuse vicious means; inferred from that ethics.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Stoics place happiness in virtue, which needs reason and philosophy rather than a simpler material life, and they took part in civic life; inferred from these principles.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Cicero discusses which trades and callings suit different people and treats a person's own role as a source of duties; inferred from that account.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Cicero holds that property exists by convention but that justice means each keeps what has become his own; inferred from On Duties.

production-for-use.rationale: Stoics treat wealth as an indifferent and Cicero scorns petty trade while accepting honest large-scale commerce; they never took a side on profit as such.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Cicero accepts gains made honestly and condemns only unjust ones; inferred from On Duties.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Marcus Aurelius praises a polity with the same law for all and freedom for the governed, against rule of one class over another; inferred.

collective-farming.rationale: Cicero praises agriculture as the best livelihood and treats land as held by convention by its owners; inferred from On Duties.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Stoics trace war and conflict to vice and false judgments such as greed and ambition, not to an economic system; inferred and anachronistic.

taxation-theft.rationale: Cicero urges rulers to avoid burdening citizens with property taxes but accepts them when the state needs them; inferred from On Duties.

harm-principle.rationale: Stoic law aims at virtue and the common good under natural law, not only at preventing harm; inferred, and modern Stoics differ.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Stoics thought in terms of duties and roles within circles of concern rather than rights held by individuals or groups; the statement is anachronistic for them.

conscription.rationale: Cicero counts defending one's country among the weightiest duties, and Roman Stoics served in war; inferred from On Duties.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Stoics praised taking part in government and opposing tyrants from within, while teaching that exile is no real evil; inferred.

state-as-business.rationale: Cicero likens government to a guardianship for the good of those governed, and Stoics treat citizens as fellow members of a common city; inferred.

media-academia-power.rationale: The statement is anachronistic for Stoicism, which says nothing about universities or news media.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Stoics hold that all human beings share reason equally by nature, even slaves; inferred, since they never addressed group differences in ability.

organic-representation.rationale: Stoic concern runs outward through family, community and country, but the school proposed no scheme of representation and the statement is anachronistic.

total-state.rationale: Marcus Aurelius praises a government that respects the freedom of the governed above all; inferred.

national-rebirth.rationale: Stoics are cosmopolitans who seek renewal in personal virtue rather than in the nation, though Roman Stoics did deplore moral decline; inferred.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Cicero holds war justified only to live in peace without injury and condemns ambition for glory and power; inferred from On Duties.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Marcus Aurelius's ideal is a polity with the same law for all, not personal bonds of dependence; inferred.

bound-labor.rationale: Stoics taught that slaves are equals by nature and should be treated humanely, yet they held legal status to be an indifferent and did not oppose servile institutions.

universal-morality.rationale: Stoics hold that one right reason pervades nature and binds all humans as citizens of a single cosmic city, the origin of natural-law theory.

single-common-good.rationale: Marcus Aurelius says what is not good for the hive is not good for the bee, and Stoics see a common reason and law serving the common good of all.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: The statement is anachronistic for Stoicism, which offers no view on any people's claim to a homeland.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: Stoicism says nothing about diaspora citizenship; its cosmopolitanism makes every person a citizen of the world rather than of a homeland.

revive-national-language.rationale: Stoicism takes no position on national languages; the statement is anachronistic for it.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Stoicism has no theory of how firms should be governed; Roman Stoics were property-owning aristocrats and modern Stoics range across the political spectrum, so this is inferred as split.

school-vouchers.rationale: Stoics stressed moral education in virtue but proposed no scheme for funding or providing schools, and modern adherents differ on school choice, so this is inferred as split.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Cicero, following the Stoic Panaetius, says the state must see that no public debt arises that harms it, while also rejecting debt cancellation; this fiscal prudence is inferred rather than a school doctrine, and modern Stoics are split on stimulus.

economic-freedom.rationale: Stoicism sets no economic program, and Cicero treats property as a matter of convention while Stoics value freedom of the governed, so this is inferred as split; modern Stoics range from market liberals to social-justice advocates.

rule-by-example.rationale: Marcus Aurelius opens the Meditations by crediting the personal example of his family and teachers for his character, and Stoic political thought pictures the wise ruler as a model of virtue; the school still accepts law, so this is agreement rather than strong agreement.

national-self-determination.rationale: Stoic cosmopolitanism makes the world city of rational beings the primary community and treats ties to one's own country as a nearer circle of duty, not a ground of entitlement to a nation-state; inferred from this, as Stoics never discussed nationhood in the modern sense.

force-without-un.rationale: Inferred and anachronistic: Cicero binds war by legitimate cause and fixed rules but names no international body to approve it, and Stoic cosmopolitanism cuts both ways, so it is treated as split.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Stoics made reason (logos) the sole standard of the good life and treated passions as errors of judgment, but they also held a providential, divine cosmos and valued duty and tradition, so reason is primary without excluding all else.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Inferred from cosmopolitanism: all rational beings are fellow citizens of one world city, so reserving help for citizens alone sits badly with Stoic duties to humanity; welfare itself is not discussed.

positive-liberty.rationale: Stoic freedom is inner mastery of one's judgments, so lacking resources does not make a person unfree.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Stoicism does not address welfare design; wealth is an indifferent and modern Stoics split on this, so it is inferred as split.

class-collaboration.rationale: Stoics stress that all share reason and a duty to the common good, so partnership is favoured over antagonism, but this is inferred.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Cicero's Stoic-influenced duties stress honouring ancestral institutions, but the school has no view on cultural policy; inferred.

dominated-front.rationale: Nothing in Stoicism addresses blocs of states; its cosmopolitanism cuts against us-versus-them alignments but does not settle the question.

workers-nation.rationale: Stoic cosmopolitanism treats all rational beings as fellow citizens of one world city, which cuts against organising primarily by nation; this is inferred.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Stoics such as Musonius held women capable of the same virtue, yet Roman Stoics accepted existing public roles, so adherents split.

ban-interest.rationale: Cicero in De Officiis quotes Cato's hostility to usury as a disreputable trade, but no Stoic source calls for a legal ban.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Stoic cosmopolitanism holds all humans share reason and one world city, which is incompatible with legally sorting and separating people by race.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Stoics see law and the state as meant to serve the common good under natural law, though they never analysed class; inferred.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Stoicism is not an energy policy; indifferents like wealth and comfort are to be used wisely, and modern Stoics may be split.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: The Roman Stoics accepted foreigners as fellow world citizens but did not discuss cultural assimilation; inferred as split.

elite-replacement.rationale: Stoics blame unreason and vice for public ills and counsel calm acceptance and tolerance of the ignorant, so a conspiracy theory of mass replacement is not supported.

proportional-representation.rationale: Stoicism offered no electoral theory; it accepted many forms of rule so long as they were just.

national-mission.rationale: Cosmopolitan Stoics regard all rational beings as fellow citizens and held no national calling, though Cicero ties Rome's rule to justice.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Musonius Rufus argued women can study philosophy and share virtue, but Stoics did not frame society as systematically structured against women; modern adherents are split.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Stoics such as Cato, Seneca and Musonius opposed tyrants, but Marcus Aurelius and Cicero's duties also urge public service; no uniform view of the political class.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Stoics hold all humans share reason and treat the rational soul as the basis of equal standing, so inferred opposition to state coercion over who has children.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Cicero's duties stress justice and Stoics condemned tyrants, but nothing addresses accountability of states for past abuses; adherents are split.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Cicero holds that the state exists to protect justice and property, but Stoics also urge a duty to the common good and Marcus's kingly rule; split on how limited the state is.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Stoic cosmopolitanism makes virtue and reason, not descent, what matters, so discouraging marriage across races is at odds with it; the ancients never addressed race in the modern sense, so this is inferred.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Marcus Aurelius praises a polity of equal rights and equal freedom of speech and holds all rational beings share one law and one city, though the Stoics did not call for abolishing slavery or hierarchy.

socialism-one-country.rationale: Stoicism has no theory of socialism or revolution, so the answer is inferred as indifferent.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: The ancient sources do not address settlement states, and modern Stoics could judge it either way, so this is inferred as split.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Marcus holds that reason and law are common to all rational beings who are fellow citizens, which suggests one law for all; inferred, as the Stoics never addressed religious personal law.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Stoic ethics treats assent as each person's own judgement and values freedom of the governed, so legal policing of belief is inferred as unlikely, although Marcus himself allowed persecution of Christians.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Stoics held that animals lack reason and exist for human use, so reverence for cattle gives no ground for a legal ban; this is inferred from that doctrine.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Stoics revered providence and the divine reason yet had no view on public schooling, and modern Stoics divide on religion, so this is inferred as split.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: Stoicism has no doctrine of socialist states; Marcus defended the empire in war yet judged rule by justice, so this is inferred as split.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Cicero and Marcus ground rule in justice, duty to the common good and the ruler's virtue, and accept monarchy that respects the governed's freedom, so consent is not the only basis; inferred.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Stoics hold that sound reason can grasp truth through assent to clear impressions, so knowledge is not simply a product of power; political application is inferred.

trade-surplus.rationale: Stoicism never addressed trade balances and treats wealth as an indifferent, so this is inferred as split.

population-transfer.rationale: Inferred: Stoic cosmopolitanism and the duty not to harm others in Cicero count against expelling people, though the school set out no rule on populations.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Cicero, following Panaetius, says the first duty of justice is that no one harm another unless provoked, but Stoics also allowed just war, so the 'whatever the goal' wording gets only mild agreement.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Stoics hold that humans are made for one another and for cooperation, so competition is not seen as the main engine of progress.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Stoicism offers no doctrine on banning parties; modern Stoics span the political spectrum, so this is inferred as split.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Inferred: Roman Stoics such as Cato and Thrasea opposed tyrants and Marcus Aurelius prized a polity with equal law and respect for the freedom of the governed.

separated-powers.rationale: Stoicism set out no constitutional design; Cicero's own view is not documented in these sources, so this is inferred as split.

vanguard-party.rationale: Inferred: Stoics hold that every rational being can reach virtue by reason, so there is no need for a leading party; the question is anachronistic.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Inferred: Cicero's Stoic-influenced ethics make property a matter of convention and warn against redistribution, and wealth is an indifferent, though beneficence to the needy is a duty.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Stoics treat property as an indifferent and gave no program on housing tenure; adherents could go either way.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Industrial relations law is far from Stoic concerns; Stoic duty to the common good and to fairness cuts both ways, so this is genuinely split.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Stoicism treats wealth and poverty as indifferents and offers no theory of poverty's causes; nothing in it settles this.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Stoic cosmopolitanism holds that all rational beings share one law and one world city and that humans are made for cooperation, so the claim that difference undermines society runs against it.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Cicero, following the Stoic Panaetius, favours rule by those of proven virtue and a mixed constitution; chance selection sits badly with the idea that the wise should hold office. Inferred.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Cicero's Stoic-influenced account insists that justice binds even in war and that expediency never overrides right; this suggests wariness of setting law aside, but emergencies are not directly discussed.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Stoicism has no economic program; duty to relieve the needy might favour it while respect for property might not, so adherents split.

party-controls-media.rationale: Stoics prized frank speech and the independence of reason from rulers (as in Stoic opposition to tyrants); control of information by authorities conflicts with that. Inferred.

party-commands-army.rationale: The Stoic duty is to the common good and the rational law of the community, not to a faction; inferred, as parties in the modern sense did not exist.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Cosmopolitanism treats everyone as a fellow citizen of the world, so heavy barriers to membership are disfavoured; Roman Stoics did not discuss residence rules, so this is inferred.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Cicero's De Officiis says office is a duty and warns against profiting from it, but sets no pay level; this is inferred as split.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Inferred: Stoics prize each person's own rational judgment and duty to reason, which sits badly with being bound to a party line.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Inferred: the Stoic sense of a single world city of rational beings favours common institutions across nations, though no Stoic text addresses a union.

head-commands-forces.rationale: The Roman Stoics served under emperors and in the republic and prescribed no constitution, so this is inferred as split.

church-by-bishops.rationale: The Stoic god is immanent reason and there is no church to govern, so this is inferred as indifferent.

clerical-rule.rationale: Authority belongs to the wise by reason, not to clergy; inferred because Stoicism has no priesthood or sacred law.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Cicero treats service to one's country as a duty of the good citizen, and Marcus Aurelius served Rome in its wars; inferred.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Stoics care about moral character but gave no doctrine on state censorship; inferred as split.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: The school never discussed re-election limits, and modern Stoics span the spectrum, so this is split.

recall-officials.rationale: Stoicism offers no view on recall; Stoics urge accountability but political mechanisms are left open.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Stoicism has no doctrine on alliances: cosmopolitanism disfavors narrow loyalty, but Cicero accepts just war and keeping treaties; inferred as split.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Cicero defends private property as a basis of justice, and wealth is an indifferent, so banning rental is not a Stoic aim; inferred.

people-in-arms.rationale: The school gave no view on military organisation; inferred as split.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Virtue lies in one's judgments, not place: Marcus tells himself the retreat he seeks in the country can be found within himself.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Stoicism is indifferent to borders and offers no doctrine on partition; inferred.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Stoics prize education and philosophical training, as Marcus thanks his teachers; the claim is not one the school makes.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: The Stoic doctrine of a shared universal reason makes all humans equal members of one world city, though Romans still valued their own culture; inferred.

death-penalty.rationale: Cicero accepts execution of traitors while Stoic emphasis on mercy and reason is later; adherents are split.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Stoics hold men and women alike capable of virtue, but the school never addressed school curricula; inferred as split.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Stoics held that a rational, providential cosmos is divinely ordered, but have no view on school curricula; modern Stoics mostly accept evolution. Inferred as split.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Stoics urge sexual self-restraint but no school doctrine on legal bans exists; inferred as split.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Stoic cosmopolitanism sets citizenship in a shared world city, with no doctrine on national rules; inferred.

minority-language-support.rationale: No Stoic doctrine on language policy; inferred.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Stoicism has no doctrine on legal exemptions for belief; inferred as split.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Stoics treat others' opinions and custom as indifferents, neither to be sought nor feared, but the school does not promote eccentricity; inferred.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Cicero's De Officiis condemns debt cancellation as unjust to creditors while Stoic cosmopolitanism pulls toward relief; inferred split.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Stoicism treats externals as indifferents and has no program of property transformation; inferred split.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Stoicism favours rule by reason and law of any form; no stance on constituent assemblies.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Wealth and growth are indifferents and Stoics prize freedom of reason, so trading liberty for growth is inferred as disfavoured.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Stoic cosmopolitanism holds duties of justice and beneficence to all humans as fellow citizens of one world city.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: No Stoic principle bears on it; adherents divide between duty to defend and cosmopolitan peace.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Stoics accepted a range of constitutions, including Marcus Aurelius's monarchy; no stance.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Technical policy not addressed; no basis for a side.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Cosmopolitanism cuts against attachment to territory but duty to country cuts the other way; inferred split.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: De Officiis holds property is private but should be used for the common good, and Modern Stoics stress this social duty.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: Anachronistic and not a Stoic question.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Prudence is a Stoic virtue, but the school gave no guidance on environmental regulation, so this is inferred as split.

collective-defense.rationale: Cicero treats keeping faith with allies and defending them as a duty of justice, so honouring a mutual-defense pledge fits Stoic duty; inferred.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Stoic justice forbids taking what belongs to others and Cicero condemns unjust aggression; the legal status question itself is inferred.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Stoicism has no church or doctrine on clergy and civil power, so adherents are split; this is inferred.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Marcus presents the good ruler as serving the whole community, not a faction, which suggests a unifying head; inferred.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Stoic duty to the common good cuts both ways between keeping a state together and avoiding violence; inferred as split.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Stoicism treats local citizenship as nested within the world city but says nothing on regional autonomy; inferred as split.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Stoics place divinity in universal reason shared by all humans, not in a ruler by descent, so a divine ruler is at odds with their egalitarian cosmopolitanism; inferred.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Wealth and status are indifferents and Stoicism set out no tax policy, so this is inferred as split.

character-from-environment.rationale: Stoics stress that character rests on our own judgments and assent, yet credit teachers and upbringing, as Marcus does in Book One; inferred as split.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: The Stoic common law of reason binds every human, rulers included, which the scholarship traces into natural law.

space-expansion.rationale: Stoicism holds that happiness lies in virtue, not in expanding power or resources, so space expansion as a central goal is unlikely to be endorsed; inferred.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Cicero, writing in the Stoic-influenced tradition of Panaetius, favoured a blend of monarchic, aristocratic and popular elements, though Stoic texts here do not make it doctrine; inferred.

leader-cult.rationale: Marcus Aurelius thanks his teachers for teaching modesty and distrust of display, and Stoics regard fame as an indifferent; inferred.

equal-parenting.rationale: Stoic duties of parents to children are affirmed, but custody rules are not addressed; inferred as split.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: Stoicism stresses harmony of reason and duty to the common good over class conflict; inferred from its social ethics.

land-redistribution.rationale: Cicero, following the Stoic Panaetius, condemns agrarian laws that take property from owners as unjust, since property is held by convention and should be respected.

refugee-return.rationale: Stoic cosmopolitanism holds that all humans are fellow citizens owed justice and help; inferred that refugees would be treated humanely.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Stoics hold fellow citizenship rests on shared reason, not nationality; inferred that nationality is no ground for a territorial claim.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Marcus Aurelius urges tolerance of the ignorant and Stoics treat belief as a matter of judgment, so legal punishment of leaving a religion does not fit; inferred.

women-must-cover.rationale: Stoicism has no doctrine of dress law and values reason and individual virtue over compulsion; inferred as a mild no.

common-currency.rationale: Stoicism does not address currency and the world-city ideal might favor unity, but adherents would not make it a doctrine; inferred as split.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Stoic belonging rests on common reason shared by all humans, not kinship or ancestry; inferred.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Stoicism is not a theory of minorities; respect for the freedom of the governed in the Meditations might support autonomy but this is inferred as split.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: Stoics are world citizens who accept circumstances and may live anywhere; they would be split on fighting for rights versus emigrating, inferred.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Stoics hold that reason and virtue, not material change, shape the good life and society; inferred.

ban-cartels.rationale: Stoicism is not an economic theory, and its view of justice in property gives no clear rule on competition policy; inferred as split.

no-bailouts.rationale: Modern Stoics span the political spectrum and the school sets no rule on rescuing failing firms; inferred as split.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Stoics hold that a natural law of reason stands above state law and that all share the same law, so no majority may override it.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Stoicism holds that office should go by virtue and does not address representation quotas; modern adherents differ, so this is inferred as split.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Marcus Aurelius sees all as citizens of one world-state, which sits badly with closing an economic bloc off; inferred.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Modern Stoics are split on trade policy and the school has no doctrine on binding trade clauses; inferred.

moral-incentives.rationale: Stoics say virtue is the only good and wealth an indifferent, and urge duty to the common good, which fits moral over material motives.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Cicero condemns Caesar's seizure of power as ambition against the law and Stoics prize duty to the lawful community; inferred.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Stoics count birth rank as a mere indifferent, so they might not defend titles nor campaign to abolish them; inferred as split.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Roman Stoics owed duties first to country and then to humanity, and cosmopolitanism pulls the other way; the school sets no curriculum, so inferred as split.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Stoics held all rational beings to be fellow citizens under one law, which sits badly with ruling others by rank, though Roman Stoics served an empire; inferred.

patriotic-education.rationale: Cicero's duty to country is strong but Stoic cosmopolitanism limits pride in one nation; modern adherents differ, so inferred as split.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Stoicism has no doctrine on this; modern Stoics divide on social justice policy, and the statement is anachronistic.

public-money-creation.rationale: Money creation is a matter of external indifferents on which Stoicism takes no side; inferred as split.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Stoicism has no economic theory, and the question of capitalism's collapse is anachronistic; inferred as split.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Stoics were cosmopolitan yet served Rome's empire; the question is anachronistic and adherents would split.

delink-world-market.rationale: Cosmopolitan Stoicism sees one human community with duties to all, which leans against severing ties; inferred.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: Wealth and status are indifferents and the school offers no class analysis; inferred as split.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: Stoics hold that humans exist for one another and that justice binds us to all people, which leans against refusing dealings on any ground; inferred.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Stoic natural-law thought and Marcus's ideal of the same law for all lean toward protected rights, but there was no written entrenched charter; inferred.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: Not addressed; Stoic justice concerns duties among all humans, but modern treaty questions are left to prudence, so inferred as split.

elective-rulers.rationale: Stoics accepted kingship, republic or empire so long as rule was just (Marcus praises a kingly government respecting freedom; Cicero favours a republic); no fixed rule on selection.

minority-veto.rationale: Inferred: the common good and law of reason bind members of the community, so a single dissenter cannot block it, though individual conscience stays free.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Stoics such as Cato, Musonius and Seneca opposed tyrants, and Cicero follows Panaetius in condemning Caesar for breaking law and trust.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Anachronistic; Stoics valued law over the arbitrary will of a ruler but had no theory of parliamentary supremacy.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Orthodox Stoics held that animals lack reason and that justice does not extend to them, so their suffering carries no direct moral weight.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Inferred from the Stoic view that animals exist for the use of rational beings; cruelty is not endorsed as a vice of character.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Cicero following Panaetius teaches that wealth and position carry duties of beneficence and service to others and to the commonwealth.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Stoics held that the wise take part in public life as a duty, in explicit contrast to the Epicurean advice to withdraw.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: Anachronistic; Stoics held that social order matters little to inner freedom and did not analyse media as a tool of domination, so mildly disagree.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: Not a Stoic theme; no basis for either answer beyond an inference of indifference to this kind of social theory.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Not addressed; Stoic indifference to wealth and the stress on personal virtue over structure suggest rejecting structural-exploitation claims.

native-born-offices.rationale: Inferred from Stoic cosmopolitanism: all rational beings are fellow citizens, though Roman Stoics held that duties to compatriots come first.

party-own-road.rationale: Question about communist parties does not apply to Stoicism; answered neutral.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: Stoic self-sufficiency applies to the individual, while the duty of beneficence toward all humans points the other way; inferred as split.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Inferred: Cicero holds war is just only to redress injury and keep faith, and Stoics rank ambition for territory as a vice.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: Inferred from the Stoic principle of one law for all and equal rational nature, which rejects descent-based political rank.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Anachronistic; modern Stoics are divided on political questions and Stoicism is not a political theory.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Anachronistic; Stoics opposed tyranny in any form but modern adherents split on this comparison.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: Historical dispute outside Stoic concern; modern adherents vary.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: Stoics treat reputation and honours as indifferents; no stance follows, and modern adherents differ.

male-disadvantage-attention.rationale: Inferred: Stoic justice and care for the common good favour attending to every disadvantaged group on its merits.

domestic-violence-symmetry.rationale: Inferred: Stoics condemn injustice and cruelty whoever suffers it, and Musonius held men and women have the same virtues.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Stoics believed in one universal law of reason yet accepted differing civil laws; inferred as split.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Inferred: Cicero holds that arms should yield to the toga and condemns Caesar for taking power by force.

paid-care-work.rationale: Not addressed; Stoic indifference to wealth and status gives no answer and modern adherents differ.

filial-duty.rationale: Roman Stoic ethics treats duties to parents and kin as appropriate acts; the school never legislated on it, so this is inferred from its doctrine of role-based duties.

office-by-exam.rationale: Stoicism says nothing on how officials are chosen; Cicero's republican ideal and Marcus's kingly rule point different ways.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Stoicism has no economic program and treats wealth as an indifferent; a cosmopolitan outlook and a duty to the homeland pull in opposite directions.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Stoicism has no doctrine of divorce; modern Stoics divide, so this is treated as split.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Nothing in the Stoic sources addresses delegate versus trustee representation; Cicero stresses office as a duty of judgment while Marcus prizes the freedom of the governed.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Pension design is an indifferent matter for Stoics and modern adherents span left and right on it.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Cicero, following Panaetius, grounds property in occupation, law and convention and says justice protects what is held, which tells against land held only while used; this is inferred.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Marcus Aurelius admires a polity under the same law for all that respects the freedom of the governed, and Cicero defends constitutional rule, so legislative control of spending is inferred as fitting.

single-official-language.rationale: The Stoic ideal of one common law of reason for all humans and a world city is hostile to making one language a restrictive sole medium; this is inferred.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: Stoic cosmopolitanism treats all humans as fellow citizens, so barring foreigners from owning land sits badly with it, though Cicero accepts civic property rules; inferred.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: Stoicism judges justice by intent and virtue of action, but also stresses care for the disadvantaged; modern Stoics divide on outcome-based tests.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Stoics call wealth and status indifferents and urge simplicity of living, so chasing possessions is a mistaken value, though they do not condemn the possessions themselves.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Cicero's just-war doctrine requires a just cause and formal declaration, and Stoic cosmopolitanism disfavours stirring up wars abroad; inferred.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Cicero condemns domination by force and unjust aggression, and Stoic cosmopolitanism respects others' standing; inferred as opposed.

missingStatements.text: There is a natural law, knowable by reason, that stands above the laws of any state.
missingStatements.rationale: Stoics hold that a common reason gives all humans a common law, and scholars trace the natural-law tradition directly to Stoicism.

notes: Stoicism is a philosophy of life rather than a political theory, so most policy answers are low-confidence inferences or splits. Early Stoicism (Zeno's Republic) was more radical and Cynic-influenced than the Roman Stoicism used here. Modern Stoics openly span the political spectrum; Scott and Pigliucci say adherents can be conservative or progressive.
